kyc01.title: The KYC message
kyc01.brief: A message arrives about your bank account. Decide what to do. Use the Scam Lens before you trust anything.
kyc01.o2: Inspect who sent it with the Scam Lens
kyc01.o3: Inspect the link before tapping it

sms.b: Update now or your account will be blocked:

lens.sender: A made-up sender code. Real banks use a registered sender ID that clearly carries their name, and anyone can fake a look-alike.
lens.today: 'Today' creates panic so you act before you think. Real KYC updates give you weeks and a letter.
lens.link: A short link hides where it goes. Banks do not ask you to update KYC through a link in an SMS.
lens.url: This address is not your bank's website. It only imitates the look of one.
lens.otp: An OTP proves it is you. Anyone who asks you to type it into a website is trying to be you.
lens.autofill: A helper that reads your messages sounds convenient. It lets the tricksters read your OTPs too.

why.sender: The sender name looked official but anyone can choose a look-alike. Check the bank app or call the number on your card.
why.urgency: Scammers rush you. Real banks do not block accounts 'today' by SMS.
why.link: Never update KYC through a link in a message. Go to the branch or the bank's own app.
why.url: The web address was not your bank's. Look carefully at the part before the last dot.
why.otp: An OTP is for you only. A bank never asks you to type it on a website or tell anyone.

page.title: Update your KYC
page.a: To keep your account active, enter your name and the OTP we just sent.
page.otp: Enter the OTP from your SMS.

perm.ask: Allow KYC Helper to read your text messages?

kyc01.explain: This is a scam. Banks do not ask for KYC through a link in an SMS, and the urgent deadline is meant to stop you thinking.

collect01.title: The cricket bat buyer
collect01.brief: You listed your old cricket bat for sale. A buyer says he is sending the money. Stay alert before you touch the PIN pad.
collect01.o3: Inspect the wording with the Scam Lens

req.pin: Enter your UPI PIN to accept.

lens.promise: He says he is sending money, but the next screen will ask you to pay him.
lens.payee: The chat was with {buyer}. This request comes from {payee}. A real buyer's name matches.
lens.wording: 'Is requesting' means money is pulled out of your account. A payment you receive never says that.
lens.pin: You only type your PIN to send money. To receive money you never need it.
lens.timer: A countdown is pressure. A genuine payment is never lost by thinking for a minute.

why.pulls: Read the first line of a payment screen. 'Requesting' means money leaves your account.
why.pin: Receiving money never needs your PIN. If a screen asks for it, money is going out.
why.mismatch: The name on the request did not match the buyer you chatted with. Check names before you pay.
why.timer: The timer is a pressure tactic. Scammers want you to act before you think.

inbox01.title: Red Flag Hunter
inbox01.brief: Six items arrived. Open each one, use the Scam Lens, then say whether it is Legit, Suspicious or a Scam.
inbox01.o2: Use the Scam Lens on a name

bank.a: ₹250 debited at Canteen on your account.
bank.b: If this was not you, call the number on the back of your card.

l.sender: A registered sender that matches your bank. Real alerts look like this.
l.amount: It only tells you what happened. There is no link and nothing to enter.

bank.explain: This is real. It only informs you of a payment you made, asks for nothing, and has no link. It also tells you to use the number on your card.

mom.a: Hi, it's Mom. My phone broke, this is my new number.
mom.b: Please send ₹5,000 to this number right now, it's urgent.

l.name: The number is not saved in your contacts. Anyone can type 'Mom' as a name.
l.urgent: 'Right now' stops you from calling to check.
l.secret: Secrets stop you asking someone who would spot the trick.

w.pretends: Call your real parent on the old number before sending anything.
w.urgency: A real emergency can wait one phone call.
w.secrecy: 'Don't tell anyone' is the loudest warning sign.

mom.explain: This is a scam. It uses a familiar name from an unknown number, creates urgency, and asks you to keep it secret. Always call the person on the number you already have.

friend.a: Bro, class trip money is due Friday. Pay at the school office, not online.

l.name: A saved contact you know. It asks nothing risky.

friend.explain: This is real. It is from a saved contact, it has no link, and it sends you to pay in person at the school office.

job.subject: Job confirmed: pay registration fee
job.a: Congratulations! You are selected for a work-from-home job at ₹40,000 a month. No interview needed.
job.b: Pay a ₹999 registration fee to confirm.

l.addr: A made-up company address with no real website behind it.
l.pay: Good pay with no interview is almost never real.
l.fee: A real employer never asks you to pay to get hired.

w.too_good: High pay for no work or interview is bait.
w.fee: Real jobs pay you. If you are asked to pay first, walk away.

job.explain: This is a scam. High pay with no interview and a fee to get hired are the two classic signs of a job scam.

call.a: Sir, I am calling from the bank's fraud team.
call.b: Your card will be blocked in 10 minutes.
call.c: Tell me the OTP you just received to stop it.

l.number: An ordinary mobile number. Banks do not call from private mobiles.
l.claim: Anyone can say they are from the bank. Hang up and call the number on your card.
l.urgent: 'In 10 minutes' is pressure to stop you thinking.
l.otp: No bank ever needs your OTP over a call.

w.pretends: Hang up and call the bank yourself on the number printed on your card.
w.urgency: Pressure is a tool. Real banks give you time.
w.otp: Never read out an OTP. It only helps the person asking.

call.explain: This is a scam. A caller who claims to be the bank and asks for your OTP is never genuine, because no bank needs your OTP.

parcel.a: Your parcel is held. Pay ₹12 customs fee:

l.sender: A courier-like code. You are not expecting a parcel, so it could be anyone.
l.link: A short link hides where it goes. The fee is small so you do not think twice.

w.link: Small fees on strange links collect your card details. Check on the courier's own app.

parcel.explain: This is suspicious. A short link and a small fee are warning signs, but nothing proves that the parcel is fake. Do not tap it; check the courier's own app first.

prize.a: Congratulations! You have won ₹25,000 in the lucky draw.
prize.b: Pay a ₹499 processing fee to claim it

l.sender: A prize-style sender code. You never entered any draw, so there is nothing to win.
l.prize: You cannot win a draw you never entered. Big prizes for nothing are bait.
l.fee: A real prize never asks you to pay first. The fee is the whole trick.
l.urgent: A short deadline pushes you to pay before you check.

w.too_good: A prize from a draw you never entered is bait.
w.fee: Real winnings never come with a fee. Paying is how you lose money.
w.urgency: The deadline stops you from checking with someone first.

prize.explain: This is a scam. You cannot win a draw you never entered, and a real prize never asks for a fee first.

task.a: Part-time job: like videos and earn ₹3,000 a day from home.
task.b: Send your bank details and we will start today.

l.name: A stranger using a friendly name. You did not apply anywhere.
l.earn: ₹3,000 a day for liking videos is not a real wage.
l.details: A genuine employer does not need your bank login or PIN to start.

w.too_good: Very high pay for very little work is bait.
w.asks_secret: Never send bank details or codes to someone you do not know.

task.explain: This is a scam. Very high pay for liking videos, plus a request for your bank details, are signs of a task scam.

school.a: School fee for term 2 is due on 15 November. Pay at the school office.
school.b: The school never asks for your PIN or OTP.

l.sender: A registered sender that matches your school. It does not ask for anything urgent.
l.office: It sends you to the school office, not to a link. Genuine messages let you verify in person.

school.explain: This is real. It is from the school's registered sender, it asks for nothing urgent, and it sends you to the office rather than a link.

whatif.title: What would have happened
whatif.mom: You sent ₹5,000 to the new number. Your real mother had never changed her number, and the money was gone within the minute.
whatif.job: You paid the ₹999 registration fee. There was no job, and a second message asked for more fees.
whatif.call: You read out the OTP. ₹8,000 left your account before the call ended.
whatif.parcel: The page asked for your card number. A few hours later ₹3,500 was spent from your account.
whatif.kyc: The fake form asked for your OTP. You typed it in and ₹4,999 left your account.
whatif.prize: You paid ₹499. A second message then asked for ₹2,000 as 'tax'. The prize never arrived.
whatif.task: They paid ₹100 for liking videos, then asked for a ₹2,000 'deposit' to unlock bigger tasks. The deposit was never returned.

inbox.title: A day in your inbox
inbox.brief: Messages arrive through the day in Messages, Chat, Mail and Phone. For each one, decide how to respond. Some are real, so do not block everything.
inbox.o2: Use the Scam Lens on something

qr01.title: Scan to receive
qr01.brief: A buyer wants to pay you and sends a QR code. Think about what scanning a code really does.
qr01.o2: Inspect the message with the Scam Lens

chat.b: Scan this code to receive the money.

lens.scan: Scanning a QR code starts a payment from you. It never receives money.
lens.direction: The screen shows you paying, not receiving.
lens.pin: Asking for your PIN confirms that money is leaving.

why.scan: You never scan anything to receive money. Share your UPI ID or QR instead.
why.direction: Check which way the money moves before you confirm anything.
why.pin: A PIN means money is leaving your account.

a.decline: Decline and share my own UPI ID

pay.pin: Enter your UPI PIN to confirm.

upi.title: UPI Simulator
upi.brief: Set up UPI, pay a canteen by QR, then face a payment request that tries to take your money. One rule matters most: you never need your PIN to receive money.

link.title: Link your bank account
link.body: The savings account from the bank counter is ready to link to Pay.

pin.setHelp: Choose four digits only you know. Avoid 1234 or repeated digits.
pin.weak: That PIN is too easy to guess. Choose another.
pin.locked: Too many wrong tries, so the payment was cancelled. Scan again.
pin.observer: Someone is standing close behind you.
pin.uncovered: You typed your PIN while someone could see it. Next time, cover the keypad first.

scan.title: Pay the canteen
scan.help: Point the camera at the canteen's QR code.

rule.title: Rule card
rule.rule: You never need a PIN to receive money.
rule.body: Your PIN is only for sending money. If a screen asks for it while money is supposed to be coming to you, money is going out instead.

refund.title: When a payment fails
refund.body: If money is deducted but the payment fails, your bank reverses it automatically within a few working days.
refund.p1: Nobody needs to call you to arrange a refund.
refund.p2: Nobody needs your PIN, OTP or a screen-sharing app.
refund.p3: If it does not return, contact your bank using the number on your card.

q1.prompt: A buyer says he is sending money. A screen asks for your UPI PIN to accept it. What do you do?
q1.a: Enter the PIN to accept the money
q1.c: Ask him to send it again
q1.why: Accepting money never needs a PIN. A request that asks for one is pulling money out.

q2.prompt: When do you need your UPI PIN?
q2.why: The PIN authorises money leaving your account. Receiving never needs it.

q3.prompt: A payment failed but the money was deducted. What happens?
q3.b: Call the number a stranger sends and share an OTP
q3.why: Failed payments are reversed by the bank. Nobody legitimate asks for your PIN or OTP to refund you.

done.title: UPI Simulator complete
done.body: You have practised paying safely, spotting a collect request, and recognising a QR trick.

hub.title: Stay Safe
hub.sub: Four simulators, each built around a different kind of trap. Pick one to practise. Everything here is simulated: no real money, no real people.

upi.title: UPI Simulator
upi.blurb: Set up Pay, pay by QR, and learn the one rule that stops collect-request and QR scams: you never need a PIN to receive money.

inbox.title: Scam Inbox
inbox.blurb: A day of messages from banks, recruiters and relatives. Decide how to respond to each one, without blocking the real ones.

hunter.title: Red Flag Hunter
hunter.blurb: Inspect messages, calls and emails with the Scam Lens and label each one Legit, Suspicious or Scam.

call.title: The Call
call.blurb: Phone calls from people who claim to be your bank or an officer. Practise keeping calm and hanging up.

judge.scam_suspicious: Suspicious keeps you safe. Scam is the stronger call, because this message has clear red flags and no good reason to trust it.
judge.suspicious_scam: Scam is a cautious, safe call. Suspicious is more accurate: there is a warning sign but nothing proves it is fake, so the right step is to check through an official app or number.
judge.unsafe: This is not a safe call. The message has red flags, and treating it as legit could lead you to tap the link, pay or share a code.
judge.false_alarm: This message is real. Calling real messages scams means you might ignore alerts and dates that matter. Doubting everything is a risk too.

scam.block: Blocking and reporting is the best response. It stops this sender and helps warn others.
scam.ignore: Ignoring is safe. Blocking and reporting is better, because ignoring leaves the scammer free to try someone else.
scam.ask: Asking a trusted adult is a good habit and safe. Once you are sure, blocking and reporting is the best next step.
scam.open: Opening or replying gives the scammer what they want. The next card shows what would have happened.

genuine.open: This message is real, so opening it is the best response.
genuine.ask: Checking with a trusted adult is safe. This one was real, so you could also have opened it.
genuine.ignore: Ignoring is safe, but this message was real. Ignoring it could mean missing something important.
genuine.block: This is a false alarm. The message was real, and blocking a real sender means you stop getting messages you need.
